title: Beyond the Sky and the Earth
author: Jamie Zeppa
blurb: A young Canadian teacher’s first impressions of Bhutan’s overwhelming landscape, written with wonder and poetic language.
source: Zeppa writes about her arrival in Bhutan as a young teacher from Canada
heading: From Beyond the Sky and the Earth: A Journey into Bhutan - Jamie Zeppa
context: When Zeppa was 24 years old she left Canada to teach in Bhutan. This memoir grew out of an essay she wrote about her early days in the country.

paragraphs.html: Mountains all around, climbing up to peaks, rolling into valleys, again and again. Bhutan is all and only mountains. I know the technical explanation for the landscape, landmass meeting landmass, the Indian subcontinent colliding into Asia thirty or forty million years ago, but I cannot imagine it. It is easier to picture a giant child gathering earth in great armfuls, piling up rock, pinching mud into ridges and sharp peaks, knuckling out little valleys and gorges, poking holes for water to fall through.

It is my first night in Thimphu, the capital, a ninety-minute drive from the airport in Paro. It took five different flights over four days to get here, from Toronto to Montreal to Amsterdam to New Delhi to Calcutta to Paro. I am exhausted, but I cannot sleep.

From my simple, pine-paneled room at the Druk Sherig hotel, I watch mountains rise to meet the moon. I used to wonder what was on the other side of mountains, how the landscape resolved itself beyond the immediate wall in front of you. Flying in from the baked-brown plains of India this morning, I found out: on the other side of mountains are mountains, more mountains and mountains again. The entire earth below us was a convulsion of crests and gorges and wind-sharpened pinnacles. Just past Everest, I caught a glimpse of the Tibetan plateau, the edge of a frozen desert 4,500 meters above sea level. Thimphu's altitude is about half of that, but even here, the winter air is thin and dry and very cold.

The next morning, I share breakfast of instant coffee, powdered milk, plasticky white bread and flavorless red jam in the hotel with two other Canadians who have signed on to teach in Bhutan for two years. Lorna has golden brown hair, freckles and a no-nonsense, home-on-the-farm demeanor that is frequently shattered by her ringing laughter and stories of the wild characters that populate her life in Saskatchewan. Sasha from British Columbia is slight and dark, with an impish smile. After breakfast, we have a brief meeting with Gordon, the field director of the WUSC program in Bhutan, and then walk along the main road of Thimphu. Both Lorna and Sasha have traveled extensively; Lorna trekked all over Europe and northern Africa and Sasha worked for a year in an orphanage in Bombay. They are both ecstatic about Bhutan so far, and I stay close to them, hoping to pick up some of their enthusiasm.

Although Thimphu's official population is 20,000, it seems even smaller. It doesn't even have traffic lights. Blue-suited policemen stationed at two intersections along the main street direct the occasional truck or landcruiser using incomprehensible but graceful hand gestures. The buildings all have the same pitched roofs, trefoil windows, and heavy beams painted with lotus flowers, jewels and clouds. One-storied shops with wooden-shuttered windows open onto the street. They seem to be selling the same things: onions, rice, tea, milk powder, dried fish, plastic buckets and metal plates, quilts and packages of stale, soft cookies from India−Bourbon Biscuits, Coconut Crunchies and the hideously colored Orange Cream Biscuits. There are more signs of the outside world than I had expected: teenagers in acid washed jeans, Willie Nelson's greatest hits after the news in English on the Bhutan Broadcasting Service, a Rambo poster in a bar. Overall, these signs of cultural infiltration are few, but they are startling against the Bhutanese-ness of everything else.

The town itself looks very old, with cracked sidewalks and faded paintwork, but Gordon told us that it didn't exist thirty-odd years ago. Before the sixties, when the third king decided to make it the capital, it was nothing but rice paddies, a few farmhouses, and a dzong−one of the fortresses that are scattered throughout the country. Thimphu is actually new. "Thimphu will look like New York to you when you come back after a year in the east," he said.

At the end of the main road is Tashichho Dzong, the seat of the Royal Government of Bhutan, a grand, whitewashed, red-roofed, golden-tipped fortress, built in the traditional way, without blueprints or nails. Beyond, hamlets are connected by footpaths, and terraced fields, barren now, climb steadily from the river and merge into forest. Thimphu will never look like New York to me, I think.

The Bhutanese are a very handsome people, "the best built race of men I ever saw," wrote emissary George Bogle on his way to Tibet in 1774, and I find I agree. Of medium height and sturdily built, they have beautiful aristocratic faces with dark, almond-shaped eyes, high cheekbones and gentle smiles. Both men and women wear their black hair short. The women wear a kira, a brightly striped, ankle-length dress and the men a gho, a knee-length robe that resembles a kimono, except that the top part is exceptionally voluminous. The Bhutanese of Nepali origin tend to be taller, with sharper features and darker complexions. They too wear the gho and kira. People look at us curiously, but they do not seem surprised at our presence. Although we see few other foreigners in town, we know they are here. Gordon said something this morning about Thimphu's small but friendly "ex-pat" community.

When we stop to ask for directions at a hotel, the young man behind the counter walks with us to the street, pointing out the way, explaining politely in impeccable English. I search for the right word to describe the people, for the quality that impresses me most−dignity, unselfconsciousness, good humor, grace−but can find no single word to hold all of my impressions.

In Thimphu, we attend a week-long orientation session with twelve other Irish, British, Australian and New Zealand teachers new to Bhutan. Our first lessons, in Bhutanese history, are the most interesting. Historical records show that waves of Tibetan immigrants settled in Bhutan sometime before the tenth century, but the area is thought to have been inhabited long before that. In the eighth century, the Indian saint Padmasambhava brought Buddhism to the area, where it absorbed many elements of Bon, the indigenous shamanist religion. The new religion took hold but was not a unifying force. The area remained a collection of isolated valleys, each ruled by its own king. When the Tibetan lama Ngawang Namgyel arrived in 1616, he set about unifying the valleys under one central authority and gave the country the name Druk Yul, meaning Land of the Thunder Dragon. Earlier names for Bhutan are just as beautiful−the Tibetans knew the country as the Southern Land of Medicinal Herbs and the South Sandalwood Country. Districts within Bhutan were even more felicitously-named: Rainbow District of Desires, Lotus Grove of the Gods, Blooming Valley of Luxuriant Fruits, the Land of Longing and Silver Pines. Bhutan, the name by which the country became known to the outside world, is thought to be derived from Bhotanta, meaning the "end of Tibet" or from the Sanskrit Bhu-uttan, meaning "highlands".

While the rest of Asia was being overrun by Europeans of varying hue but similar cry, only a handful of Westerners found their way into Bhutan. Two Portuguese Jesuits came to call in 1627, and six British missions paid brief but cordial visits from the late 1700s until the middle of the next century. Relations with the British took a nasty turn during the disastrous visit of Ashley Eden in 1864. Eden, who had gone to sort out the small problem of Bhutanese raids on British territory, had his back slapped, his hair pulled, and his face rubbed with wet dough, and was then forced to sign an outrageous treaty that led to a brief war between the British and the Bhutanese. Considering the consolidated British empire in the south, and the Great Game being played out in the north between the colonial powers, Bhutan's preservation of its independence was remarkable. I am full of admiration for this small country that has managed to look after itself so well.

bhutan-only.quote: Bhutan is all and only mountains
bhutan-only.what: After a long opening sentence, this short one lands bluntly, and 'all and only' allows nothing else.
bhutan-only.effect: The mountains fill every view, so they fill the sentence too.

cannot-imagine.what: Zeppa knows the science of colliding landmasses but admits she cannot picture it.
cannot-imagine.effect: Facts fail to capture Bhutan for her, which sets up the playful image that follows.

giant-child.quote: giant child gathering earth in great armfuls, piling up rock, pinching mud into ridges and sharp peaks, knuckling out little valleys and gorges, poking holes for water to fall through
giant-child.what: The small, hand-sized verbs 'pinching', 'knuckling' and 'poking' turn mountain-building into a child playing with mud.
giant-child.effect: The vast landscape becomes easy to picture, and feels freshly made.

five-flights.quote: five different flights over four days
five-flights.what: Counting flights and days, then listing every city, makes the sentence feel as long as the journey.
five-flights.effect: We feel how remote Bhutan is, and how far she is from home.

exhausted-cannot.quote: I am exhausted, but I cannot sleep
exhausted-cannot.what: Two short clauses pull against each other: her body is worn out, but her mind will not rest.
exhausted-cannot.effect: We sense excitement mixed with nerves on her first night.

simple-pine.what: 'Simple' and the natural 'pine' wood describe a plain, modest room.
simple-pine.effect: Nothing inside distracts her from the mountains outside the window.

mountains-moon.quote: mountains rise to meet the moon
mountains-moon.what: The mountains 'rise to meet' the moon, as if moving on purpose to greet a friend.
mountains-moon.effect: The night feels magical, seen by someone already under the landscape's spell.

baked-brown.what: 'Baked' suggests an oven, so India's plains seem scorched, dry and flat.
baked-brown.effect: They make a sharp contrast with Bhutan's cold, jagged mountains, like entering another world.

mountains-more.quote: on the other side of mountains are mountains, more mountains and mountains again
mountains-more.what: Zeppa answers her childhood question by repeating 'mountains' four times in one clause.
mountains-more.effect: The sentence seems endless, like the view, and the answer is gently funny.

convulsion.quote: convulsion of crests and gorges and wind-sharpened pinnacles
convulsion.what: A 'convulsion' is a violent shaking of the body, as if the earth froze mid-spasm.
convulsion.effect: The mountains feel wild and restless, a darker picture than the playful giant child.

tibetan-plateau.quote: Tibetan plateau, the edge of a frozen desert 4,500 meters above sea level
tibetan-plateau.what: 'Frozen desert' sounds like a contradiction, since we link deserts with heat.
tibetan-plateau.effect: With the exact height, it makes the plateau seem vast, empty and almost unreal.

thin-dry-cold.quote: thin and dry and very cold
thin-dry-cold.what: Repeating 'and' between adjectives, called polysyndeton, slows the list and builds to 'very cold'.
thin-dry-cold.effect: The air feels harsh and hard to breathe, showing the physical challenge of living here.

instant-coffee.quote: instant coffee, powdered milk, plasticky white bread and flavorless red jam
instant-coffee.what: Every food is processed, and 'plasticky' is the sharpest word, suggesting bread that is barely food.
instant-coffee.effect: The dry humour brings us down to earth after the magical mountains.

no-nonsense.what: The hyphenated adjectives 'no-nonsense' and 'home-on-the-farm' make Lorna sound sensible and down to earth.
no-nonsense.effect: Her manner is then 'shattered' by laughter, revealing a warmer, wilder side.

ringing-laughter.what: 'Ringing' makes her laugh sound like a bell: loud, clear and hard to ignore.
ringing-laughter.effect: Lorna's confidence makes Zeppa's own quiet nerves stand out.

slight-dark.quote: slight and dark, with an impish smile
slight-dark.what: 'Impish' comes from 'imp', a mischievous sprite, so Sasha seems playful and full of fun.
slight-dark.effect: Small, playful Sasha contrasts with sturdy Lorna, each sketched in a few words.

ecstatic.what: Zeppa gives the extreme word 'ecstatic' to the others and pointedly does not claim it herself.
ecstatic.effect: Their delight makes her own doubts stand out.

stay-close.quote: I stay close to them, hoping to pick up some of their enthusiasm
stay-close.what: 'Pick up' makes enthusiasm sound catching, like a cold she hopes to get.
stay-close.effect: Her honest nerves make her easy to relate to for anyone who has started somewhere new.

no-traffic.quote: It doesn't even have traffic lights
no-traffic.what: 'Even' shows Zeppa expected traffic lights in any capital city.
no-traffic.effect: We see Thimphu through Western eyes, and the short sentence lands like a raised eyebrow.

incomprehensible-graceful.what: 'But' turns the phrase from confusion to admiration: she cannot understand the gestures, yet finds them beautiful.
incomprehensible-graceful.effect: The policemen seem almost like dancers, showing her respect for the unfamiliar.

lotus-jewels.what: Three traditional Buddhist designs decorate even ordinary beams.
lotus-jewels.effect: The town feels sacred and lovely, in contrast with the cheap goods in the shops below.

stale-soft.what: Biscuits should be crisp, so 'stale' and 'soft' show they have sat a long time after travelling from India.
stale-soft.effect: The funny, honest detail reminds us Bhutan relies on imported goods.

hideously-colored.what: 'Hideously' wildly exaggerates a biscuit's colour, adding to the comedy of the brand names.
hideously-colored.effect: Zeppa's humour makes her a friendly, honest guide.

acid-washed.what: Acid-washed jeans, a 1980s Western fashion, surprise Zeppa on Bhutanese teenagers.
acid-washed.effect: They raise a question running through the passage: can Bhutan keep its own identity?

willie-nelson.what: An American country singer straight after the news is a juxtaposition (two unlike things side by side).
willie-nelson.effect: The funny mismatch shows Western culture reaching even this remote kingdom.

rambo-poster.quote: a Rambo poster in a bar
rambo-poster.gist: An action hero in a bar
rambo-poster.what: Rambo, a violent American film hero, feels jarring in a calm Buddhist country.
rambo-poster.effect: It completes a list of three Western imports: clothes, music and film.

startling.what: 'Startling' suggests a jolt: the Western signs are 'few', yet they still jump out.
startling.effect: We sense she values Bhutan's difference and feels uneasy when the West intrudes.

bhutanese-ness.what: Zeppa invents a word, a neologism, because no ordinary word covers what she means.
bhutanese-ness.effect: It names a quality she feels but cannot define.

cracked-faded.what: 'Cracked' and 'faded' let us assume, as Zeppa did, that the town is ancient.
cracked-faded.effect: This sets up the surprise that it is new, showing how first impressions mislead.

didnt-exist.quote: it didn't exist thirty-odd years ago
didnt-exist.what: Gordon's fact overturns the old look of the town: it is only about thirty years old.
didnt-exist.effect: We are caught out with Zeppa and warned not to judge by appearances.

nothing-but.quote: nothing but rice paddies, a few farmhouses, and a dzong
nothing-but.what: 'Nothing but' and 'a few' shrink the list so it sounds almost empty.
nothing-but.effect: We grasp how quickly a capital city grew out of farmland.

actually-new.what: 'Actually' shows Zeppa adjusting to a fact that goes against what she sees.
actually-new.effect: We share her realisation, and sense Bhutan will keep surprising her.

look-like-ny.quote: Thimphu will look like New York to you when you come back after a year in the east
look-like-ny.what: Gordon's exaggeration means the east of Bhutan is so rural that tiny Thimphu will seem busy.
look-like-ny.effect: It hints at how remote Zeppa's real posting will be.

grand-whitewashed.what: Four adjectives move our eye from the white walls up to the golden tip.
grand-whitewashed.effect: The rich colours make the fortress splendid against the town's 'faded paintwork'.

without-blueprints.what: The short, plain phrase lets an impressive fact speak for itself.
without-blueprints.effect: Bhutan's old ways seem skilled and wise, matching Zeppa's growing respect.

never-look.quote: Thimphu will never look like New York to me, I think
never-look.what: Zeppa echoes Gordon's words but adds 'never', quietly disagreeing with him.
never-look.effect: She already loves Thimphu as it is, and 'I think' keeps the reply in her head.

best-built.quote: the best built race of men I ever saw
best-built.what: Zeppa quotes George Bogle, travelling through in 1774, in the language of his time.
best-built.effect: The old source adds weight, showing the Bhutanese have impressed visitors for centuries.

i-agree.what: 'I find' suggests she has looked carefully and reached Bogle's conclusion herself.
i-agree.effect: Past and present agree, which makes her description seem more trustworthy.

beautiful-aristocratic.quote: beautiful aristocratic faces with dark, almond-shaped eyes, high cheekbones and gentle smiles
beautiful-aristocratic.what: 'Aristocratic' suggests nobility, and the list of features builds a portrait of graceful people.
beautiful-aristocratic.effect: Sharp readers may notice an outsider praising looks, which edges towards treating the Bhutanese as exotic.

kira.quote: kira, a brightly striped, ankle-length dress
kira.what: Zeppa names the 'kira', then explains it in a short phrase after the comma.
kira.effect: Readers learn the local word and can picture it, without being lectured.

gho.quote: gho, a knee-length robe that resembles a kimono
gho.what: Comparing the 'gho' to a kimono uses something her readers are more likely to know.
gho.effect: She guides outsiders from the familiar to the new.

look-curiously.quote: look at us curiously, but they do not seem surprised
look-curiously.what: 'But' balances two reactions: interested, yet unbothered, as if they have seen foreigners before.
look-curiously.effect: For a moment the gaze is reversed, and Zeppa is the one being watched.

ex-pat.what: Quotation marks around 'ex-pat' (a foreigner living abroad) show Zeppa borrowing Gordon's word and keeping her distance.
ex-pat.effect: She does not yet see herself as part of that group.

impeccable-english.what: 'Impeccable' means flawless, and the young man even walks them out to help.
impeccable-english.effect: It quietly corrects any idea that a remote country must be backward.

dignity-grace.what: Four qualities with no 'and' (asyndeton) read as if she is trying one word after another.
dignity-grace.effect: We watch her think on the page, and no word is enough.

no-single-word.quote: no single word to hold all of my impressions
no-single-word.what: 'Hold' treats words like containers too small for what she feels.
no-single-word.effect: It echoes 'I cannot imagine it': Bhutan keeps going beyond her words.

most-interesting.what: The superlative shows the history lessons grip her more than anything else.
most-interesting.effect: She is moving from tourist to learner, preparing us for the history ahead.

druk-yul.quote: Druk Yul, meaning Land of the Thunder Dragon
druk-yul.what: 'Thunder Dragon' joins a force of nature with a mythical beast.
druk-yul.effect: Bhutan sounds powerful and legendary, fitting a small country that stood up to bigger ones.

just-as-beautiful.what: Zeppa judges the old names by their sound, enjoying the language as well as the facts.
just-as-beautiful.effect: We sense her falling for Bhutan through its words.

southern-land.what: This Tibetan name describes Bhutan by what grows there, suggesting a land that heals.
southern-land.effect: The capital letters make it sound like a title from a legend.

south-sandalwood.what: Sandalwood is a sweet-smelling, valuable wood, so the name brings in the sense of smell.
south-sandalwood.effect: Bhutan seems rare and precious, and the soft 's' sounds are pleasant to say.

rainbow-district.quote: Rainbow District of Desires, Lotus Grove of the Gods, Blooming Valley of Luxuriant Fruits, the Land of Longing and Silver Pines
rainbow-district.what: Each name mixes nature with feeling, through words such as 'Desires', 'Gods' and 'Longing'.
rainbow-district.effect: Bhutan starts to sound like a paradise from a fairy tale.

overrun-europeans.quote: overrun by Europeans of varying hue but similar cry
overrun-europeans.what: 'Overrun' makes colonisers sound like pests, and 'similar cry' says every nation wanted the same thing.
overrun-europeans.effect: Zeppa's wit judges empire, making Bhutan's escape seem even more impressive.

brief-cordial.what: 'Brief but cordial' suggests visitors were welcome, as long as they did not stay long.
brief-cordial.effect: The amused tone sets up the much ruder visit that follows.

nasty-turn.what: 'Nasty turn' is a casual phrase that signals the history is about to change.
nasty-turn.effect: The chatty tone makes history feel like gossip, so we lean in.

back-slapped.quote: back slapped, his hair pulled, and his face rubbed with wet dough
back-slapped.what: The three insults build from a slap to the absurd wet dough on his face.
back-slapped.effect: The comedy makes a powerful British official look foolish.

preservation-remarkable.quote: Bhutan's preservation of its independence was remarkable
preservation-remarkable.what: 'Remarkable' sums up how unlikely it was for Bhutan to stay free between rival empires.
preservation-remarkable.effect: This judgement leads straight into her personal admiration.

full-admiration.quote: I am full of admiration for this small country that has managed to look after itself so well
full-admiration.what: 'Look after itself' sounds homely, as if Bhutan were a capable person.
full-admiration.effect: Her tone ends far from the nervous newcomer: she is now an admirer.

demeanor.meaning: How someone acts and carries themselves.
demeanor.note: This is the American spelling. In British English it is 'demeanour'.
demeanor.effect: It sums up Lorna's steady, practical manner in one word.

trefoil.meaning: A shape with three rounded parts, like a clover leaf.
trefoil.note: It is a decorative shape used in windows and carvings.
trefoil.effect: The detail shows how carefully even ordinary Bhutanese buildings are decorated.

shamanist.meaning: To do with shamanism, a religion based on spirits.
shamanist.note: A shaman is a person believed to talk with the spirit world.
shamanist.effect: It shows that Buddhism in Bhutan blended with older local beliefs.

felicitously.meaning: In a pleasing and well-chosen way.
felicitously.note: It comes from the Latin word for 'happy'. A felicitous name fits perfectly.
felicitously.effect: It shows how much Zeppa delights in Bhutan's place names.

overview.heading: Why Zeppa wrote this
overview.intro: Her aims shift as the passage moves on.

points.label: To share first impressions
points.text: "It is my first night in Thimphu" shows her recording fresh, personal reactions as they happen.

points.label: To teach readers about Bhutan
points.text: "without blueprints or nails" shows her passing on facts about Bhutanese culture and skill.

points.label: To praise Bhutan's independence
points.text: "Bhutan's preservation of its independence was remarkable" shows her admiration for a small country that stayed free.

overview.heading: Who she is writing for
overview.intro: She writes mainly for Western readers who have never been to Bhutan.

points.label: Readers new to Bhutan
points.text: "a knee-length robe that resembles a kimono" shows her explaining local things through familiar comparisons.

points.label: Fans of travel writing
points.text: "I am exhausted, but I cannot sleep" shows she shares her feelings as well as the sights.

points.label: Readers curious about change
points.text: "teenagers in acid washed jeans" shows her interest in how Western culture is reaching Bhutan.

overview.heading: How her tone changes
overview.intro: Her voice grows warmer and more confident as the passage goes on.

points.label: Wonder-struck observer
points.text: "I cannot imagine it" shows her amazed by a landscape too big to grasp.

points.label: Nervous newcomer
points.text: "hoping to pick up some of their enthusiasm" shows her unsure and looking to others for confidence.

points.label: Delighted by words
points.text: "just as beautiful" shows her enchanted by Bhutan's old names and their meanings.

points.label: Impressed admirer
points.text: "I am full of admiration" shows her ending with warm respect for the country.

overview.heading: Key language choices
overview.intro: Zeppa mixes playful images with sharp, funny detail.

points.label: Childlike imagery
points.text: "giant child gathering earth" turns hard geology into a playful, magical scene.

points.label: Sensory detail
points.text: "plasticky white bread" and "stale, soft cookies" show the cheap, tired food with gentle humour.

points.label: Poetic names
points.text: "Rainbow District of Desires" makes Bhutan's place names sound like something from a fairy tale.

points.label: Juxtaposition
points.text: "Willie Nelson" set against "lotus flowers" shows modern Western culture clashing with old tradition.

overview.heading: How it is organised
overview.intro: The passage moves from landscape to people to history.

points.label: Opening with landscape
points.text: "Bhutan is all and only mountains" sets the scene with one blunt, short sentence.

points.label: Personal to historical
points.text: The passage moves from her own first days in Thimphu to Bhutan's long history.

points.label: A surprise twist
points.text: "it didn't exist thirty-odd years ago" overturns her first impression of an ancient town.

points.label: Ending with admiration
points.text: "I am full of admiration" closes the passage on her settled respect for Bhutan.
